seoTitle: How to Create a Rich Filter in Jira (Setup Guide)
metaDescription: Install Rich Filters for Jira Dashboards, build a JQL-backed smart filter, and see what the app costs once its 30-day trial ends.
intro:
Standard Jira filters are static lists; they don't let you layer conditions or hand viewers a set of clickable options the way a real dashboard needs. Rich Filters for Jira Dashboards, an Atlassian Marketplace app built by Appfire, adds a smart filtering layer on top of your existing filters that plugs straight into dashboard gadgets.

This guide covers installing the app, building a rich filter around JQL-backed smart clauses, and adding it to a dashboard, along with what the app costs once its trial period ends, which the marketing copy doesn't mention upfront.
prerequisites: Jira Cloud with permission to install Marketplace apps
An existing saved Jira filter to use as the rich filter's base
costNote: Rich Filters for Jira Dashboards is free to trial for 30 days, with a free tier for very small sites (roughly 1 to 10 users). Past that, Cloud pricing scales with user count. Appfire's 2026 pricing lists it well above $500 a year for a 25-user site, so check the current tier on the Marketplace listing before building a dashboard workflow your team depends on.

steps.heading: Install Rich Filters from the Atlassian Marketplace
steps.body: From your Jira sidebar, open Apps, then Explore more apps, and search for Rich Filters for Jira Dashboards. The listing shows its rating and install count, plus an overview video of dynamic dashboards and gadgets, worth a quick watch before installing. Click Add to install; this step needs Jira site-admin permission. Once added, it shows up under the Apps menu as Rich Filters.

image.caption: The Rich Filters for Jira Dashboards listing on the Atlassian Marketplace, showing its rating, install count, and an overview video of dynamic dashboards.

steps.heading: Create a new rich filter
steps.body: Open Rich Filters from the Apps menu and click Create rich filter. The dialog asks for a Name and a Jira filter to base it on. This base filter narrows down the issues the rich filter starts from, so pick an existing saved filter that already scopes to the right project or board. You need permission to use that filter, not ownership of it, so a shared team filter works fine here.

image.caption: The Create rich filter dialog, with a Name field and a Jira filter dropdown used to select the base filter the rich filter will build on.

steps.heading: Build a smart clause with JQL
steps.body: Inside the new rich filter, open its filter configuration and click Create smart clause. Give the clause a name and color, then write the condition in the JQL field; Jira autocompletes matching values as you type, for example suggesting status names after typing `status = `. Name each clause for what a viewer would want to click, not for its JQL syntax, since that name is what appears on the dashboard.

image.caption: The Create a smart clause dialog, with a JQL field showing autocomplete suggestions for a status condition.

steps.heading: Edit clauses as your reporting needs change
steps.body: Reopen any clause through Edit smart clause to rewrite its JQL, for instance swapping a status condition for a date range or a custom field. This is routine maintenance, not a sign something broke. A clause built around a status or field that later gets renamed keeps running but quietly returns nothing, which is worth checking for now and then.

image.caption: The Edit smart clause dialog, showing an existing clause's JQL being changed to reference a different condition.

steps.heading: Add the rich filter to a dashboard
steps.body: From any Jira dashboard, click Add gadget, search for the Rich Filters gadget, and select the filter you built. Viewers see your named smart clauses as clickable options instead of a JQL box, and results update the moment they switch between them. This is the payoff for naming clauses clearly in the step above.

troubleshooting.problem: A rich filter's clause suddenly returns nothing
troubleshooting.cause: The JQL references a status, field, or value that no longer exists, usually after a workflow or scheme change.
troubleshooting.fix: Reopen the clause under Edit smart clause and update the JQL to match the current field or status names.

troubleshooting.problem: Rich Filters doesn't appear in the Apps menu after someone installed it
troubleshooting.cause: Installing a Marketplace app requires Jira site-admin permission. Without it, the install doesn't complete even though no error shows.
troubleshooting.fix: Have a site admin install it from Explore more apps.

troubleshooting.problem: A teammate can see the app but can't build a rich filter
troubleshooting.cause: They don't have permission to use the base Jira filter that was selected.
troubleshooting.fix: Share the base filter with them, or have them build on a filter they already have access to.

faq.question: Is Rich Filters for Jira Dashboards free?
faq.answer: Only for a 30-day trial, plus a free tier for very small sites of roughly 1 to 10 users. Beyond that it's a paid Marketplace subscription that scales with user count.

faq.question: Do I need admin access to create rich filters?
faq.answer: Installing the app requires Jira site-admin permission, but once it's added, anyone with permission to use the base filter can create their own rich filters.

faq.question: Can I share a rich filter with my team?
faq.answer: Yes. Rich filters get added to dashboards as gadgets, so anyone with access to that dashboard can see and use the smart clauses you built.

faq.question: Why did a smart clause stop returning results?
faq.answer: Usually because the JQL references a status or field that's since been renamed or removed. Reopen it under Edit smart clause and update the condition.

faq.question: How is a rich filter different from a basic search?
faq.answer: A rich filter is built from named, JQL-backed smart clauses plugged into a dashboard gadget, so viewers click between saved conditions instead of typing or re-running JQL.

faq.question: Can I edit a clause after creating it?
faq.answer: Yes, through Edit smart clause. You can rewrite the JQL entirely, for example changing a status condition into a date-range check.
